title: Pottery studio kiln and expansion planning

messages.content: You are a helpful assistant experienced in ceramics and small-business operations, supporting a pottery studio owner planning a facility expansion.

Hey, I run Terra & Ash Pottery Studio and we're at a turning point, outgrowing our current kiln setup, thinking about expanding the space, and trying to get our glaze safety practices tightened up before we take on more students. I'd like to use this chat as an ongoing planning partner across all of it: kilns, glazes, scheduling, expansion, marketing. Sound good?
Good question. Let me lay out the main considerations.

Let's start with the kiln situation since it's the most urgent. We currently run a single 7-cubic-foot electric kiln and it's the bottleneck for everything else. What should I be weighing as I look at either a second kiln or upgrading to something bigger?
Happy to dig into that. Here's the short version.
For glaze chemistry, a few of our glazes are pre-mixed commercial ones and a few are ones I mix in-house from raw materials. Should I be testing for anything differently between those two categories?
Sure, a few things are worth weighing there.

Another definitions thing: at Terra & Ash, when I say 'open studio' I don't mean drop-in hours for the public. It specifically means our after-hours keyholder access for currently enrolled students only, no walk-ins, no guests.
Got it, I'll keep that in mind as we plan.
On class scheduling, we run beginner wheel, intermediate wheel, and handbuilding as separate tracks. How many weeks is typical for a beginner wheel session before people are ready to move up?
Let's think that through. There are a couple of angles.

Kiln decision time. We looked at three routes: (1) buying a second identical 7-cubic-foot electric kiln, (2) upgrading to one large 10-cubic-foot electric kiln and selling the old one, or (3) adding a small test kiln plus keeping the current one for full loads. After running the numbers, we're going with option three, the small test kiln alongside the existing one.
Understood. That's a useful constraint to work within.
Studio expansion: we're looking at knocking through to the unit next door to add some square footage. What should that extra space prioritize, more wheels or a dedicated glazing area?
Great thing to nail down early. Here's how I'd approach it.

Honestly, my personal take is that we should phase out most of our in-house mixed glazes over the next year, even the ones students love, because the safety recordkeeping burden isn't worth it for a studio our size. Commercial pre-mixed is just less risk.
Noted, thanks for flagging it clearly.
Marketing-wise, we've mostly relied on word of mouth and a small Instagram. Is it worth investing in a proper email newsletter at our size?
Worth pausing on. The key tradeoffs are pretty clear.

I've decided against hiring a dedicated part-time glaze technician position. I looked at the budget and it's cheaper and honestly simpler to just have the two senior instructors split glaze-mixing duties between them. That role is off the table for now.
Makes sense. I'll factor that in going forward.
Back to kilns, how often should we actually be doing a full cone-pack test versus trusting the kiln's own controller readout?
Let me give you a practical take on that.

Correction on the wheel count, I told you earlier we have 10 pottery wheels total, but I recounted and two of them are actually retired hand-building tables we repurposed, so we only have 8 working wheels right now.
Clear enough, I'll hold to that.

The old 10-cubic-foot kiln we're thinking of retiring, the crew nicknamed it 'Vader' years ago because it always runs about 30 degrees hotter than its dial says and has scorched more than one glaze batch. When I say Vader I mean that specific kiln.
Good to have that pinned down. Noted.
For glaze safety, do we need a respirator on hand for anyone mixing raw glaze materials, or is good ventilation enough?
Reasonable question, and the answer depends on a couple of factors.

Quick terminology note so we're on the same page going forward: when I say 'the long table' I don't mean the big communal work table, I mean specifically the glazing table against the back wall where we keep test tiles. Just want that clear before it comes up again.
Understood, I'll keep it straight from here on.
Scheduling follow-up, should instructors be paid a flat rate per class or per student enrolled?
Here's how I'd frame it for a shop your size.

On instructor pay, we weighed three structures: (1) flat rate per class regardless of enrollment, (2) per-student rate with a minimum guarantee, or (3) a hybrid, flat rate for beginner classes and per-student for intermediate. We landed on the hybrid, option three.
Thanks for the clarity, that helps the planning.
On expansion, how much lead time should I expect between signing a lease amendment and actually being able to start knocking through the wall?
Solid one to sort out now rather than later.

Just so you know where I stand: I think 8 students per wheel class is already too many for one instructor to give real feedback to, and I'd rather cap it at 6 even if it means slightly less revenue per session.
Right, I'll treat that as settled.
For marketing, is it worth running a 'clay night' date-night style event to bring in new people who aren't already into pottery?
Good question. Let me lay out the main considerations.

One idea I'm ruling out entirely: doing a mobile pottery van that goes to schools and events. I looked into the insurance and equipment costs and it's just not worth it for us right now, so let's take that off the table completely.
Noted and locked in on my end.

Quick correction on square footage, earlier I said the new unit next door is 400 square feet, but I finally got the actual lease survey back and it's really 340 square feet after accounting for the shared utility closet. Use 340 going forward.
Got it, I'll keep that in mind as we plan.

I've been calling our new glaze recipe project 'Frodo' internally, just a codename so I don't have to keep typing 'the matte celadon reduction recipe' every time. From now on when I say Frodo, that's the one I mean.
Understood. That's a useful constraint to work within.
Back to the kiln question, once we do get the second one installed, how should we stagger firing schedules between the two so we're not wasting electricity?
Happy to dig into that. Here's the short version.
When you mention the long table, use it the way I defined it before, not just any table.
Noted, thanks for flagging it clearly.
Whenever open studio comes up later, remember it's the keyholder-only meaning we defined, not public drop-in.
Makes sense. I'll factor that in going forward.
On the kiln decision we made, no need to walk through the options again, what test kiln brand would you actually suggest?
Sure, a few things are worth weighing there.
For the instructor pay structure we settled on, don't recap it, just tell me what percentage split feels fair for the per-student part.
Clear enough, I'll hold to that.
Given how I feel about class sizes, does the new studio layout still work?
Let's think that through. There are a couple of angles.
Keeping my view on glazes in mind, should the new glazing area still have a raw materials mixing station?
Great thing to nail down early. Here's how I'd approach it.
Any update on Frodo? Last test tile came out flatter than I wanted.
Good to have that pinned down. Noted.
Should we keep Vader around as a backup even after the new kiln arrives?
Worth pausing on. The key tradeoffs are pretty clear.
For glaze safety, should new students get any kind of safety orientation before they're allowed to touch raw glaze materials at all?
Let me give you a practical take on that.
On scheduling, how do we handle a waitlist fairly when a popular class fills up in a day?
Reasonable question, and the answer depends on a couple of factors.
Quick one on expansion, do we need a separate ventilation permit for the new glazing area or does it fall under the existing one?
Here's how I'd frame it for a shop your size.
Last thing, should we time the studio expansion announcement to coincide with a marketing push, or keep them separate?
Solid one to sort out now rather than later.
That covers the ground we set out to. Happy to pick any thread back up whenever you're ready.
